docs.text: A small wiki about logarithms — their history, their mathematics, and the different things they measure.

docs.title: Logarithmic scales
docs.text:
Many measurement scales are logarithmic, compressing quantities that span orders of magnitude into a linear range.

Scale Measures Definition Decibel power / amplitude ratio \(10\log_{10}(P/P_0)\) pH acidity \(-\log_{10}[\mathrm{H}^+]\) Richter / moment magnitude earthquake size \(\log_{10}\) of amplitude Stellar magnitude brightness \(-2.5\log_{10}\) of flux Thermodynamic entropy number of microstates \(k_B \ln \Omega\)

Related phenomena:

  • Benford's law — the leading digit \(d\) occurs with frequency \(\log_{10}(1 + 1/d)\).
  • Weber–Fechner law — perceived intensity scales with the logarithm of stimulus intensity.

docs.title: Continued logarithms
docs.text:
A continued logarithm expresses a number through nested logarithms, for example

\[ \log_b\!\big(d_1 + \log_b\!\big(d_2 + \log_b(d_3 + \cdots)\big)\big). \]

The term names two distinct constructions — see two lineages. The gallery plots use the nested-logarithm representation of Neunhäuserer, computed by tools/clogs.py.

docs.title: Two lineages
docs.text:
"Continued logarithm" names two different objects.

Gosper (1972). A binary "recursive scientific notation," introduced to represent numbers whose continued fractions are impractical. Developed by Borwein, Calkin, Lindstrom, and Mattingly (2016), who found an elementary analogue of Khinchin's constant.

Neunhäuserer. For base \(m \ge 3\) and digits \(d_k \in \{1,\dots,m-1\}\),

\[ [(d_k)]_m = \lim_{n\to\infty} \log_m\!\big(d_1 + \log_m(d_2 + \cdots + \log_m d_n)\big), \]

a representation of every real number in \([0,1]\). Each map \(T_d(x) = \log_m(d+x)\) is a contraction on \([0,1]\), so the limit exists.

docs.text:

docs.title: Complex logarithms
docs.text:
For a nonzero complex number \(z = re^{i\theta}\), the logarithm is

\[ \log z = \ln r + i(\theta + 2\pi k), \qquad k \in \mathbb{Z}. \]

It is multivalued: every nonzero \(z\) has infinitely many logarithms, differing by integer multiples of \(2\pi i\). The principal value \(\operatorname{Log} z = \ln r + i\theta\) takes \(\theta \in (-\pi, \pi]\), with a branch cut along the negative real axis. The full logarithm lives on a Riemann surface — an infinite spiral over the plane.

The complex logarithm turns multiplication (including rotation and scaling) into addition, just as the real one does — the basis for the Escher print gallery.

docs.text:

docs.title: The Escher print gallery
docs.text:
M. C. Escher's lithograph Prentententoonstelling ("Print Gallery," 1956) shows a man looking at a print of a harbour town that contains the gallery he is standing in — a self-referential loop with a blank patch at its centre that Escher left unfilled.

B. de Smit and H. W. Lenstra showed that the image is built from a straight, self-similar (Droste) picture warped by a conformal map. The warping is generated by the complex exponential and its inverse, the complex logarithm: in log-space the picture's self-similarity is a simple repetition, and exponentiating back turns an endless zoom into a closed loop. The Droste scaling factor is 256.

docs.text:

docs.title: The logarithm
docs.text:
The logarithm base \(b\) of a number \(x\) is the exponent to which \(b\) must be raised to give \(x\):

\[ \log_b(x) = y \iff b^y = x. \]

It is the inverse of exponentiation, defined for \(x > 0\) and base \(b > 0,\ b \neq 1\).

docs.title: Common bases
docs.text:
• Base 10 — the common logarithm, \(\log_{10}\).
  • Base \(e\) — the natural logarithm, \(\ln\).
  • Base 2 — the binary logarithm, \(\log_2\), used in information and complexity.

docs.title: See also
docs.text: • From products to sums

docs.title: The natural logarithm
docs.text:
The logarithm to base \(e = 2.71828\ldots\), written \(\ln\).

\[ \ln x = \int_1^x \frac{dt}{t}, \qquad \frac{d}{dx}\ln x = \frac{1}{x}. \]

The base \(e\) arises as the area under the hyperbola \(1/t\) and as the limit \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(1 + \tfrac{1}{n}\right)^n\).

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Grégoire de Saint-Vincent, Nicholas Mercator (17th century) — area under the hyperbola.
  • Leonhard Euler, Introductio in analysin infinitorum (1748).

docs.title: From products to sums
docs.text:
The defining property of the logarithm:

\[ \log_b(xy) = \log_b(x) + \log_b(y). \]

Up to a constant factor, \(\log\) is the only continuous function satisfying \(f(xy) = f(x) + f(y)\) — the unique map carrying multiplication to addition (a homomorphism from the positive reals under multiplication to the reals under addition).

Consequences:

\[ \log_b\!\left(\tfrac{x}{y}\right) = \log_b x - \log_b y, \qquad \log_b(x^k) = k\,\log_b x, \qquad \log_b x = \frac{\log_a x}{\log_a b}. \]

docs.title: See also
docs.text: • Napier — the property that motivated the invention.

docs.title: Briggs and base 10
docs.text:
Henry Briggs proposed rebasing Napier's logarithms so that \(\log 1 = 0\) and \(\log 10 = 1\), giving the common (base-10) logarithm. He published tables in Arithmetica Logarithmica (1624).

Base-10 logarithms were the dominant tool for numerical computation — through printed tables and the slide rule — until electronic calculators.

docs.title: Napier
docs.text:
John Napier introduced logarithms in Mirifici Logarithmorum Canonis Descriptio (1614). The name joins Greek logos (ratio, reckoning) and arithmos (number).

Napier defined the logarithm kinematically: two points move along lines, one at constant speed, the other at a speed proportional to its remaining distance to an endpoint. The logarithm relates the position of one point to the position of the other, mapping a geometric (multiplicative) progression onto an arithmetic (additive) one — see from products to sums.

docs.title: Complexity and addressing
docs.text:
To specify one item out of \(N\) requires \(\log_2 N\) bits — the length of an address, or the number of yes/no questions in an optimal search.

  • Binary search locates an item in a sorted array of \(n\) elements in \(O(\log n)\) comparisons, halving the range at each step.
  • Tree height. A balanced binary tree over \(n\) leaves has height \(\Theta(\log n)\).
  • LOGSPACE (L) is the class of problems solvable with \(O(\log n)\) working memory — enough to hold a constant number of pointers into the input, but not to copy it.

\(O(\log n)\) is the cost of locating something among \(n\) items, as distinct from reading them (\(O(n)\)).

docs.title: Dimension and capacity
docs.text:
A space of dimension \(d\) holds exactly \(d\) mutually orthogonal directions. If directions need only be nearly orthogonal, the number that fit grows exponentially in \(d\): roughly \(e^{cd}\) vectors with pairwise inner product below a fixed tolerance (Johnson–Lindenstrauss). The dimension is then the logarithm of the number of distinguishable directions:

\[ d \approx \tfrac{1}{c}\,\log(\text{capacity}). \]

Related facts:

  • \(n\) bits index \(2^n\) states; the Boolean cube \(\{0,1\}^n\) has \(2^n\) vertices, and \(n = \log_2\) of that count.
  • \(n\) qubits span a \(2^n\)-dimensional Hilbert space; the Holevo bound limits the classical information recoverable from them to \(n\) bits.
  • Superposition — networks represent many more features than dimensions by assigning nearly-orthogonal directions to features that are rarely active at once.

docs.title: References
docs.text:

  • Elhage et al., "Toy Models of Superposition" (2022). https://transformer-circuits.pub/2022/toy_model/index.html

docs.title: Information and entropy
docs.text:
The information content of an event of probability \(p\) is \(-\log_b p\); with \(b = 2\) it is measured in bits. Rarer events carry more information.

The Shannon entropy of a distribution is the expected information:

\[ H = -\sum_i p_i \log_b p_i. \]

For \(N\) equally likely outcomes, \(H = \log_b N\). The logarithm is forced by the requirement that information from independent sources add: \(I(pq) = I(p) + I(q)\) — see from products to sums.

docs.text:

  • Christopher Olah, "Visual Information Theory" (2015). https://colah.github.io/posts/2015-09-Visual-Information/

docs.title: Length
docs.text:
The base-\(b\) logarithm measures how many digits a number uses. A positive integer \(n\) has \(\lfloor \log_b n \rfloor + 1\) digits in base \(b\); \(\log_b n\) itself gives a continuous "length" that includes fractional digits.

For example, \(\log_{10} 103 \approx 2.01\) and \(\log_{10} 981 \approx 2.99\): both are three-digit numbers, but the logarithm distinguishes how fully each uses its three digits.
